Malaria Detection¶

Executive Summary:¶

  • Multiple CNN architectures were evaluated for malaria detection, including a custom base CNN, two improved CNN variants, and two transfer-learning models (VGG16 and EfficientNetB0), using both original and augmented datasets.

  • The Base Model achieved reasonable performance (97% accuracy) but produced a high number of false negatives (51), which is dangerous in medical diagnosis since infected patients could be missed.

  • Model-1 significantly improved performance with 98% accuracy, the lowest loss (0.04), and the fewest false negatives (14), indicating strong learning but also suggesting possible overfitting due to training on highly clean, idealized data.

  • Model-2, trained on augmented data, showed improved generalization but became more conservative, increasing false negatives to 40 and reducing accuracy to 96%, reflecting the expected trade-off between robustness and sensitivity.

  • VGG16, despite being a powerful pretrained model, performed worse on augmented data with 95% accuracy, 43 false negatives, and the highest false positives (83), indicating limited adaptation to the specific medical image domain and high model complexity.

  • EfficientNetB0 achieved the best overall balance with 98% accuracy, low loss (0.06), only 21 false negatives, and 31 false positives, making it the most reliable model under realistic, augmented conditions.

  • In terms of deployment feasibility:

    • Model-1 is lightweight (3.4 MB) but less robust to real-world variability.
    • Model-2 and VGG16 are too large (56 MB and 70.1 MB respectively) for practical deployment.
    • EfficientNetB0 offers an ideal trade-off between size (48.6 MB) and performance, making it suitable for real-world malaria screening systems.

  • Since real clinical data is noisy, unbalanced, and far less clean than curated datasets, EfficientNetB0’s performance on augmented data indicates better real-world robustness than models trained only on ideal images.

Final proposed model specifications¶

  • Therefore, EfficientNetB0 is selected as the final model, as it provides:

    • High accuracy
    • Low false negatives
    • Good generalization
    • And practical deployability
    • Accuracy: 98%
    • Loss: 0.06
    • FN: 21 ; FP:31
    • Model size: 48.6 MB

In conclusion, EfficientNetB0 delivers the best combination of diagnostic reliability and deployment readiness, making it the most suitable model for real-world malaria detection applications.

Summary of the Problem definition:¶

Context:¶

Malaria remains a critical global health threat in 2026 according World Malaria Report(2024) by the World Health Organization (WHO), because it can progress from mild flu-like symptoms to a fatal condition within 24 hours if untreated. Its danger stems from a multi-stage parasitic infection that systematically attacks vital bodily systems. Malaria had an estimated 282 million cases and 610 000 deaths in 2024 – roughly 9 million more cases than the previous year.

Challenges:¶

There are many challenges such as drug resistence, rising global burden, insecticide resistence etc. for Malaria. However, there are two that equally crucial ones that as a data scientist and engineer can be addressed using the capabilities of neural network and deep learning:

  1. Detection Challenges: According to WHO World Malaria Report, the parasites have evolved and no longer produce the proteins targeted by standard Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs), due to deletion of pfhrp2/3 genes. These gene deletions reduce or eliminate the target protein that HRP2-based RDTs detect, meaning infections can be missed by rapid tests.

According to WHO surveillance, these deletions have been confirmed in at least 40 countries, representing a significant global diagnostic challenge

  1. Field Realities: In WHO E-2030 goals, it is stated that malaria depends on moving diagnosis out of big cities and into remote villages Eg, sub saharan Africa. Many remote clinics lack electricity for advanced lab gear.

How Deep learning models help overcome above to challenges:¶

  1. Detection Challenges: Unlike RDTs, image-based CNN models don’t rely on a single biochemical marker (like HRP2 protein).They learn visual patterns of infected red blood cells, which still exist even if HRP2 isn’t expressed. This means the model could catch infections that RDTs miss, especially in regions where mutated parasites are prevalent.

  2. Field Realities: Modern CNNs can be optimized into "lightweight" models (like MobileNet or 2-layer architectures) that run locally on low-end smartphones. By attaching a smartphone to a basic microscope eyepiece, a community health worker can get a diagnostic result in minutes without needing an internet connection or expert advice.

Proposed Project Solution Pipeline¶

  1. Perform Exploratory data analysis on the given data set.

    • Perform data visualizations to understand the data better
    • Assert if any data preprocessing is needed, and if needed how to perform it.

  2. Model Development: In this section, different models are trained and built to see which one is the best. In total of 5 models are being tried.

    • Base Model: Built from scratch, with focus on the given task of image classification keeping in mind its future deployablity on a resource constraint platform.
    • Model_1: Based on the performance of base model, more architectural based additions may be done in this model.
    • Model_2: Based on the performance of previous models, changes in dataset, or activiation function or architecture of the model will be done to see the differences.
    • VGG-16: This model is used to test transfer learning approach and see its benefits and performance with pre-trained model weights.
    • EfficientNetB0: Based on literature survey done for this capstone problem statement, it was discovered that this pre-trained model is used and tested before for this same task, and is lightweight for deployment. Hence in this notebook, this model is also implemented.

  3. Model Training: Every aforementioned model is trained on the given dataset.

  4. Model Evaluation: For model comparisons we use different performance evaluation values to assess different aspects of model's performance.

    • Val_accuracy vs Training_accuracy charts, to see if the model is overfitting or not based on any plausible gaps between both. See the overall performance over each epoch.
    • Confusion matrix, especially to see the false negatives since they are most important implying that patient was infected but not actually detected.
    • Classification report to understand the precision, recall, f1 score of the models for comparison
    • In the end we also plot a ROC curve and calculate the AUC of the curve to see the best performing model.

  5. Conclusion of the project: In the end based on the results it is concluded which model is finalised.

Reasoning for the proposed solution:¶

  • The project helps find the better trade-off between a model that is deployable and efficiently identifies the image of a red blood cell as that of an infected one or not.
  • In this pipeline, we compare the performance of different models using different performance metrics and then download and analyze the size of these models as well, to find the correct trade-off between a lightweight model and an accurate model.

How it would affect the problem/business?¶

Based on the work done in the milestone project, it is revealed that the EfficientNet B0 is the model that provides the best performance on augmented data making the model robust and lightweight for deployment as well.

The solution of this project helps in solving the major two above mentioned challenges of the disease:

  1. RDTs independent detection of Malaria
  2. Deployment of the model to remote places like sub saharan africa in healthcare tools/wearables, where access to medical help and advanced lab gear is not easy.

Observation & Insights:¶

The dataset is highly balanced across both training and testing sets.

Training Set: There is a near-equal distribution between Class 0 (12,584) and Class 1 (12,374).

Testing Set: There is a perfect 50/50 split, with exactly 1,300 samples for each class.

Implications:

  • The model is unlikely to develop a majority-class bias, as it will receive equal exposure to both classes during training.
  • Accuracy will be a reliable performance metric in this case. Unlike imbalanced datasets, where a model can achieve high accuracy by simply guessing the majority class, here a high accuracy score will truly reflect the model's ability to distinguish between classes.
  • Other than normalization, resizing and potential data augmentation in any future model, there isn't any explicit pre-processing required to be done on the provided dataset.

# Function to find the mean
def find_mean_img(full_mat, title):

    # Calculate the average
    mean_img = np.mean(full_mat, axis = 0)[0]

    # Reshape it back to a matrix
    plt.imshow(mean_img)

    plt.title(f'Average {title}')

    plt.axis('off')

    plt.show()

    return mean_img

Observation & Insights¶

  • Clearly applying mean to the image is not useful, as it removes the textural and edge based varience in the image between the unifected and infected image. Making it hard for the model to learn anything for the distinguishing.

  • Note#1: Gaussian blurring was not applied as a standard preprocessing step, as malaria parasite detection relies on fine-grained texture and morphological features that may be suppressed by smoothing operations. Since convolutional neural networks are inherently capable of learning noise-robust representations, blurring was instead considered only as a mild data augmentation technique to simulate focus variability in microscopy images.

  • Note #2: Since this is a binary classification problem, labels are kept in binary format (0/1) and a sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy loss is used.

Model Building¶

Now that the data preprocessing and exploration is done, next step is to build various Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models to see the performance of the models and better choose the one deploying.

To acheive fairness in different models' comparison, it is carefully ensured that all models were trained under identical experimental conditions.

These include:

  1. Same train/val split (80-20)
  2. Same optimizer (Adam, LR= 0.0001)
  3. Same BATCH_SIZE (16)
  4. Same IMAGE_SIZE (96x96)
  5. Same NO_OF_EPOCHS (7)
  6. Same Loss Function = binary_crossentropy
  7. Same Callbacks Logic
    • Patience = 5
    • Monitor = val_loss (Early Stopping, when applied)
    • Monitor = val_accuracy (ModelCheckpoint, when applied)

The improvement in the model is noted via:

  1. Architecture depth
  2. Number of filters
  3. Activation functions
  4. Batch Normalization
  5. Data augmentation
  6. Transfer learning vs scratch
  7. Using different pretrained models

Base Model:¶

The proposed base CNN model is a relatively simple but effective deep learning architecture for binary image classification (Parasitized vs Uninfected red blood cells).

  • The model uses three convolutional blocks with increasing filter sizes (32 → 64 → 128), allowing it to:

    • Capture low-level features such as edges and textures in early layers.

    • Learn higher-level spatial patterns such as parasite shapes and cell abnormalities in deeper layers.

  • MaxPooling layers reduce spatial dimensions, helping:

    • Lower computational cost

    • Improve translation invariance

  • The fully connected dense layer (128 neurons) combines extracted features for decision-making.

  • The final sigmoid activation outputs a probability for binary classification.

# Build base CNN model
base_model = Sequential([

    Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', input_shape=(96, 96, 3), padding = 'same'),
    MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

    Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu',padding = 'same'),
    MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

    Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu',padding = 'same'),
    MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

    Flatten(),

    Dense(128, activation='relu'),

    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

Observations & Insights:¶

  • For any medical diagnosis project, taking look at the false negatives is crucial as that means these many patients were not detected when they actually had Malaria. And in the current model this number is very high.

  • We must focus in the upcoming model variations to see if this number is decreased or not.

Observation & Insights:¶

From the accuracy vs epochs plot:

  • Training accuracy increases rapidly from ~77% to ~98%

  • Validation accuracy closely follows training accuracy and stabilizes around 96–97%

  • The small gap between training and validation curves indicates:

    • Good generalization

    • No significant overfitting

  • The validation accuracy continues to improve gradually, suggesting the model learns meaningful features rather than memorizing data.

Precision (0.99)

When the model predicts a cell as Parasitized, it is correct 99% of the time.

Indicates low false-positive rate.

Recall (0.96)

The model correctly identifies 96% of infected cells.

Very important for malaria screening to avoid missing infected cases.

Conclusion: The model converges well and maintains stable performance on unseen data for a base model. The dataset is highly balanced and well-curated, which makes the classification task less noisy and allows the model to achieve high performance.

It would be interesting to see if adding Batch Normalization and LeakyReLU changes the accuracy more or not. Hence we move towards the next model Model_1

Model 1¶

Architectural Changes and Their Purpose¶

Compared to the base CNN, Model-1 introduces three key improvements aimed at better robustness and real-world applicability:

(a) Batch Normalization¶

  • Added after every convolutional and dense layer
  • Stabilizes activation distributions during training
  • Allows higher learning rates and faster convergence

(b) LeakyReLU Activation¶

  • Replaces ReLU to avoid the dying ReLU problem
  • Maintains small gradients for negative inputs
  • Improves gradient flow, especially in deeper networks

(c) Increased Depth¶

  • More convolutional layers (5 conv blocks vs 3 in base model)
  • Enables learning of more complex and hierarchical features
  • Makes the model more expressive and closer in spirit to VGG-style architectures

(d) ModelCheckpoint¶

  • Ensures the best-performing model (on validation data) is saved
  • Prevents degradation due to late-epoch overfitting

Observations and Insights:¶

As we note the learnable parameters have decreased from before, which is likely due to Batch Normalization as the training is more targettedly generalized.

Due to decrease in the learnable parameters, the size of the model has also decreased significantly, which can be useful for deployabilty of the model.

The accuracy and overall performance metrics of this model would reveal more insights.

Observation:¶

The false negatives have decreased from 51 → just 14, which is a huge improvement.

The false positives have increased, however it seems better trade off, as false negatives are far more dangerous.

Observation & Insights:¶

  • Clearly the loss has decreased from 0.064 → 0.042
  • The accuracy also has improved from 97.9% to 98.3%
    • Better confidence calibration
    • Improved feature representation
  • The precision has decreased to 0.98 for parasitized from 0.99, which seems a fair trade of because the False positives have decreased significantly in this model.
  • The size of this model is 3.2 MB which is lesser than previous model, increasing its potential for deployability after careful prunning etc.
  • Closely following graph of val_accuracy with Training accuracy indicates that there is not overfitting.

Next Steps:

Although the dataset is clean and balanced, real-world blood smear images often vary in illumination, orientation, staining, and noise. Data augmentation artificially introduces such variations, helping the model learn more generalizable features rather than relying on dataset-specific patterns. This improves robustness when the model is applied to unseen or real clinical data.

Hence the next model will be fed augmentated data, along with also applying early stopping to perserve model computation resources.

Model-2 (Hybrid Pooling CNN) – Architecture Description¶

This model extends the previous CNN by using hybrid pooling, where Max Pooling and Average Pooling are applied in parallel after each convolution block and their outputs are concatenated. Max Pooling helps capture the most prominent parasite-related features, while Average Pooling preserves overall texture and contextual information of red blood cells.

Each block consists of Conv2D + Batch Normalization + LeakyReLU, which improves training stability, prevents dying ReLU issues, and reduces overfitting. The increasing number of filters (32 → 64 → 128) allows the model to learn progressively more complex features.

By combining pooled features through concatenation, the model retains richer representations without significantly increasing depth. The final dense layers perform binary classification using a sigmoid activation.

Overall, this architecture is designed to be more robust to real-world variations (noise, illumination, staining differences) compared to simpler CNNs, while still remaining lightweight.

In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import AveragePooling2D, Concatenate,Input
from tensorflow.keras.models import Model

input_layer = Input(shape=(96, 96, 3))

# ---- Block 1 ----
x = Conv2D(32, (3,3), padding='same')(input_layer)
x = BatchNormalization()(x)
x = LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.1)(x)

max_p = MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2,2))(x)
avg_p = AveragePooling2D(pool_size=(2,2))(x)
x = Concatenate()([max_p, avg_p])

# ---- Block 2 ----
x = Conv2D(64, (3,3), padding='same')(x)
x = BatchNormalization()(x)
x = LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.1)(x)

max_p = MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2,2))(x)
avg_p = AveragePooling2D(pool_size=(2,2))(x)
x = Concatenate()([max_p, avg_p])

# ---- Block 3 ----
x = Conv2D(128, (3,3), padding='same')(x)
x = BatchNormalization()(x)
x = LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.1)(x)

max_p = MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2,2))(x)
avg_p = AveragePooling2D(pool_size=(2,2))(x)
x = Concatenate()([max_p, avg_p])

# ---- Classifier ----
x = Flatten()(x)
x = Dense(128)(x)
x = LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.1)(x)

output = Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')(x)

model_2 = Model(inputs=input_layer, outputs=output)

Observations & Insights:¶

  • The size of this model is 56.2MB, which is very high and would need proper prunning and quantization to be make it remote device deployable friendly.

  • The accuracy of this model has decreased from previous 98% (Model_1) and 97% (Base_model) to 96%, which is expected since the model was fed augmentated data.

  • Higher accuracy of previous can be associated with models learning the inherent patterns of the dataset itself and not actually learn the textural varience, which implies Model_2 is more robust than previous ones with 96% accuracy.

  • The loss has increased from 0.04 to 0.10, which is very significant.

  • Other performance metrics can help get more insights.

Observation & Insights:¶

  • The classification report however interestingly remains the same; this can be attributed to the rounding of evaluation metrics and the averaging effect over a large test set, which masks the underlying variation in misclassification patterns observed in the confusion matrices.

  • So we look at the confusion matrix, and clearly the FN from previous lowest value 14 has increased to 40. Hence the model 2 is making more wrong classifications.

  • While the augmented model shows reduced sensitivity, this trade-off improves robustness, as real-world blood smear images are far less clean and controlled than the curated dataset provided, making the augmented model more reliable under realistic conditions.

  • The size of this model is 56 MB, which makes it more for non-remote deployment in the labs, where the RDTs might fail with detecting, this model has better chances to detect the disease. However, careful architecture changing and basic quantisation and pruning techniques can also make this model deployable for remote healthcare devices.

Next Steps:

In the next section of the notebook, pre-trained models are implemented to see if there is any change in the performance compared to model_2.

Based on above it is concluded that even though model_1 and base_model perform well with the given dataset, model_2 is expected to perform better and is more robust.

In the next section it is noted if any of the two pre-trained models perform better than model_2.

VGG-16 Pre-trained Model¶

In this work, VGG16 is used as a feature extractor through transfer learning. The pretrained convolutional layers capture generic visual patterns such as edges, textures, and shapes, which are highly transferable to medical images like blood smears. A custom classification head is added on top of the frozen base network to adapt VGG16 to the binary malaria detection task.

In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras import backend
backend.clear_session()
In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras.applications import VGG16
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dropout, Dense, Flatten

vgg_base = VGG16(
    weights='imagenet',
    include_top=False,
    input_shape=(96, 96, 3)
)
for layer in vgg_base.layers:
    layer.trainable = False

x = vgg_base.output
x = Flatten()(x)

x = Dense(256, activation='relu')(x)
x = Dropout(0.5)(x)

x = Dense(128, activation='relu')(x)
x = Dropout(0.3)(x)

output = Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')(x)

Observation & Insights:¶

  • There is clear alarming rise in the FN and FP, 43 and 83 respectively. The classification report also reports lower values in comparison to mdoel_2's performance.

Implication and insight:

Although VGG16 is a strong pretrained model, its features are learned from natural images (ImageNet), which differ significantly from microscopic blood cell images. Data augmentation further altered the appearance of cells, making it harder for VGG16’s pretrained filters to adapt, leading to higher false positives and false negatives compared to Model-2, which was trained directly on augmented malaria images from scratch

This highlights a key limitation of transfer learning: pretrained models do not always generalize well compared to a CNN built from scratch when the target domain differs significantly from the source domain, especially under aggressive augmentation.

Next Steps:

Since we noted that using a pretrained model weights (ImageNet) from a differnt source domain didnt helped much. According to the literature survey done for this project, in the next section will work with a pretrained model whose weights are specifically trained for medical imaging tasks.

EfficientNetB0¶

In this project, EfficientNetB0 is chosen as a lightweight yet powerful transfer-learning model, motivated by its prior success in medical image classification tasks reported in literature and its suitability for deployment in practical malaria screening systems.

A custom classification head is added on top of the pretrained EfficientNetB0 backbone to adapt the model to the binary task of parasitized vs uninfected red blood cell classification.

In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras.applications import EfficientNetB0
from tensorflow.keras.layers import GlobalAveragePooling2D
In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras.applications.efficientnet import preprocess_input

train_gen = ImageDataGenerator(
    preprocessing_function=preprocess_input,
    validation_split=0.2
)

test_gen = ImageDataGenerator(
    preprocessing_function=preprocess_input
)
In [ ]:
base_cnn = EfficientNetB0(
    weights="imagenet",
    include_top=False,
    input_shape=(96, 96, 3)
)

base_cnn.trainable = False  # warm-up phase

model_effnet = Sequential([
    base_cnn,
    GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
    BatchNormalization(),
    Dense(128),
    LeakyReLU(),
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

ROC Curve and checking the AUC¶

Comparing Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models using ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curves is a standard method for evaluating and visualizing their classification performance. The primary metric for comparison is the Area Under the Curve (AUC), where a higher AUC value indicates superior performance

In [ ]:

y_true = test_generator.classes
In [ ]:

y_prob_effnet = model_effnet.predict(test_generator).ravel()

auc_vgg = auc(fpr_vgg, tpr_vgg)

fpr_effnet, tpr_effnet, _ = roc_curve(y_true, y_prob_effnet)
auc_effnet = auc(fpr_effnet, tpr_effnet)

Clearly according to the graph EfficientNetB0 has a very comparable performance with model_1 however, EffcientNetB0 works with augmented data making it also more robust.

Recommendations for Implementation¶

Key Recommendations for Implementing the Proposed Solution¶

  1. Adopt EfficientNetB0 as the baseline deployment model Based on comparative evaluation, EfficientNetB0 demonstrated the best balance between accuracy (98%), low false negatives (21), generalization on augmented data, and manageable model size (48.6 MB). It is therefore recommended as the core diagnostic model for real-world malaria screening applications.

  2. Deploy the model on edge devices using post-training optimization techniques Direct deployment of a 48.6 MB model on microcontrollers (such as STM32 F/H series boards with ~564 KB–1.4 MB RAM) is infeasible. Hence, model pruning and quantization should be applied to reduce memory footprint and inference latency while preserving diagnostic accuracy.

  3. Integrate the model with smartphone-based microscopy systems The most practical deployment strategy is to run the optimized model on low-cost Android smartphones attached to basic microscope eyepieces, enabling offline inference in remote clinical settings.

  4. Use augmented data during training to improve real-world robustness Since clinical data is noisy and variable, future retraining should prioritize augmented datasets to avoid overfitting and ensure reliable performance under field conditions.

Key Actionables for Stakeholders, Expected Benefits, and Costs¶

Stakeholder Key Actionables Expected Benefits Expected Costs
Healthcare Providers Adopt smartphone-based screening tools Faster diagnosis, reduced dependency on lab infrastructure Initial device procurement
NGOs & Public Health Agencies Deploy systems in remote clinics Improved early detection, reduced mortality Training and logistics
ML Engineers Apply pruning, quantization, and benchmarking Smaller models, faster inference Engineering effort
Policy Makers Approve AI-assisted diagnostics Scalable malaria screening Regulatory evaluation

Key Risks and Challenges¶

  1. False Negatives in High-Stakes Medical Diagnosis Despite strong performance, even a small number of false negatives can have serious consequences. Continuous monitoring and threshold tuning are required.

  2. Domain Shift Between Training Data and Real Clinical Images Differences in staining quality, microscope resolution, and lighting conditions may reduce model performance in practice.

  3. Hardware Constraints in Ultra-Low-Power Devices While smartphones are feasible, direct deployment on microcontrollers remains challenging without aggressive optimization.

  4. Regulatory and Ethical Constraints AI-based medical tools require validation, explainability, and approval from health authorities before clinical adoption.

Further Analysis and Future Work¶

  1. Model Compression Techniques Apply pruning, post-training quantization (INT8), and knowledge distillation to reduce EfficientNetB0’s size, enabling deployment on constrained edge devices.

  2. Clinical Validation Studies Test the model on real blood smear samples collected from multiple regions to evaluate generalization and bias.

  3. Explainability and Trust Building Integrate techniques such as Grad-CAM to visualize infected regions and increase clinician trust in predictions.

  4. Comparison with Ultra-Light Models Evaluate architectures such as MobileNetV3 or custom shallow CNNs for extreme low-resource environments.

  5. End-to-End Deployment Pipeline Develop a complete pipeline including image acquisition, preprocessing, inference, and result reporting for field deployment.

Final Implementation Perspective¶

While EfficientNetB0 cannot be directly deployed on microcontrollers due to severe memory limitations, its performance makes it an excellent candidate for optimized edge deployment. Through pruning and quantization, the model can be significantly reduced in size while maintaining diagnostic reliability. When combined with smartphone-based microscopy, this solution provides a scalable, robust, and practical approach to malaria detection in resource-limited settings, directly addressing critical gaps in current diagnostic systems.
